description_full: BrasilAgro - Companhia Brasileira de Propriedades Agrícolas engages in the acquisition, development, exploration, and sale of agricultural properties in Brazil, Paraguay, and Bolivia. It operates through six segments: Real Estate, Grains, Sugarcane, Cattle Raising, Cotton, and Other. The company is involved in the cultivation of soybean, corn, cotton, bean, sorghum, sugarcane, cattle raising, and cotton lint and seed, as well as pasture; and production and sale of beef calves after weaning. It also engages in production, sale, import, and export of agriculture products and inputs, cattle raising and forestry activities; purchases, sells, and rents real estate in rural and/or urban properties; and sale of the raw products. In addition, the company provides real estate brokerage services; manages third-party assets; and operates farms through own and leased lands. BrasilAgro - Companhia Brasileira de Propriedades Agrícolas was incorporated in 2005 and is headquartered in São Paulo, Brazil.

financial_summary: Brasilagro Brazilian Agric Real is a small-cap consumer defensive business with a $312M market cap on $152M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -12% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 10% against a 7% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it. Gross margins of 74% confirm genuine pricing power.
The company is burning through $1M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.5×.

Management returns a meaningful 8.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 24% operating margin runs 16pp above the Consumer Defensive median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.92x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-6.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 30% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.39, it is more defensive than the market.
Trading is thin (about $181K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 49% in the 2020 crash and 47% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 70%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 28.5 vs 18.3 and EV/EBITDA 55.1 vs 10.2 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 9% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -0.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.4% (vs the 8% bar).
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 6.7%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.58).
It runs a 74% gross margin and burns cash (FCF margin -1%).
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.4x net debt to EBITDA ($25.3M of cash against $93.9M of debt), with interest covered 6.5x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.83 in the distress zone.
The value-trap profile is elevated (58/100); see the breakdown below.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -11.8% over 3 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 36%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and institutions hold 8%.
Insider trading is two-way: 12 purchases and 3 sales over the past year, net $581K bought.
It returns 8.7% a year to shareholders (1.9% in dividends).
The share count has grown 10.2% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 143% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
